title: Why Chip Stocks Are Crashing & What It Means for the AI Trade
creator: Couch Investor
source_note: Detailed summary generated from video captions; panel discussion, captions garbled in places
summary: Couch Investor hosts a panel debate: have chip and bottleneck stocks genuinely topped, or is this sentiment-driven selling? A friend at a large-cap semiconductor firm asks: with record bullish capex, earnings, free cash flow and buybacks, why are semiconductor stocks still depressed? Panellists weigh geopolitics, bond yields, the Iran war and midterm-year volatility against something deeper in the trade itself. Applied Optoelectronics (AOI) is the running example: a June high near $250, now around $70-80, with buyers at $158 hoping for a double that may never come. Micron is the key disagreement: one panellist still calls it an investment that will break new highs on cash generation and buybacks, while others argue memory names are trades, not investments, because their moat is timing and the cycle always ends in overbuilding. Nvidia is treated differently, with a defensible moat in its ecosystem and roughly 75% gross margins. Marvell (MRVL) is discussed as up 144% year to date yet unable to hold its gains, with some arguing it barely deserves the $200s. The panel notes that 2018 and 2022 were ugly midterm years while 2019 and 2023 were big up years, and that sentiment can flip violently, citing Bloom moving from $190 to $230 within two days of earnings. No recommendation is issued; Micron is mentioned only as a holding the host still believes will break new highs, which is treated as UNCERTAIN, not a call. Tickers discussed: MU, AOI, MRVL, NVDA, AMD, plus large caps AMZN, GOOGL and META.
